stories.title: ULA's Vulcan rocket fails about 10 minutes after lifting off from Cape Canaveral on 15 Nov, destroying all 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites on the first of 38 Vulcan launches Amazon has bought; ULA says it suffered an 'anomaly' and has no data yet on the cause, Ars Technica's sources place the problem in the BE-4-powered booster stage, and the rocket, which carries about half of upcoming US national-security launches, is expected to be grounded indefinitely
stories.h: ULA's Vulcan rocket fails minutes after launch, destroying all 40 Amazon Leo satellites
stories.sub: The first of 38 Amazon launches ends in ULA's first mission failure; the Pentagon's second rocket is likely grounded.
stories.ticker: ULA's Vulcan fails on launch; 40 Amazon Leo satellites lost
stories.body:
United Launch Alliance's Vulcan lifted off from Cape Canaveral at 12:40 pm EDT on 15 Nov carrying 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites, and failed about 10 minutes into flight; all 40 were lost (Ars Technica, The Verge). ULA said the rocket "suffered an anomaly" and "failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit", that it did not yet have data on the cause, and that "today, we did not meet that standard." Ars Technica's sources say the fault was in the booster stage, powered by two Blue Origin BE-4 engines, not the upper stage or the six solid boosters. The Verge reports it as ULA's first mission failure in 20 years. It was the first of 38 Vulcan launches Amazon has bought; Amazon said ULA has been a trusted partner and it expects ULA to learn from the flight.

So what: Vulcan carries about half of the US military's planned national-security launches and most of Amazon's plan to catch Starlink. An indefinite grounding leaves SpaceX, which caught its Starship upper stage a day earlier, even more dominant, and pushes Amazon Leo's rollout back again.
stories.chip: Checked on Ars Technica and The Verge (ULA's and Amazon's statements, time, booster-stage detail) and ULA's own mission page (40 satellites, first of 38 Amazon launches); ULA's failure statement itself was posted on X, which we did not open
stories.brief:
Vulcan's six solid rocket boosters, which had failed on two of its four earlier flights, worked this time. The trouble came later: Ars Technica's sources say the core booster stage, powered by two methane-burning BE-4 engines from Blue Origin, had a problem before the 10-minute mark when ULA says the anomaly occurred. ULA has not said what failed and says customers will see the investigation.

The loss matters well beyond one launch. Vulcan is one of two rockets certified for US national-security missions, and Amazon had booked 38 Vulcan flights to build Leo, its Starlink rival, which ULA's mission page says will start with more than 3,000 satellites. Ars expects the rocket to be grounded for an indefinite period while the cause is found.
facts: Vulcan failed about 10 minutes after liftoff; 40 Amazon Leo satellites lost

stories.impactWho: Amazon and its Leo customers; the US Space Force and other national-security launch customers; Blue Origin (BE-4 supplier); SpaceX's competitors and investors in its planned listing.
stories.short: ULA's Vulcan rocket failed about 10 minutes after launch on 15 Nov, destroying all 40 Amazon Leo satellites on the first of 38 Amazon flights. ULA says it does not yet know why; Ars Technica's sources point to the BE-4-powered booster stage. The rocket is expected to be grounded.

stories.title: The Bank of England, the Monetary Authority of Singapore and the Bank of Thailand publish the results of Project Meridian FX APAC (13 Nov): a prototype 'synchronisation operator' built by Partior settled payment-versus-payment FX and multilateral net FX across their RTGS and DLT test systems, and the BoE says the findings feed its plan for a live synchronisation interface in 2028
stories.h: Three central banks show FX trades settling across different systems at once
stories.ticker: BoE, MAS and Bank of Thailand test synchronised FX settlement; BoE live service planned for 2028
stories.body:
The Bank of England, the Monetary Authority of Singapore and the Bank of Thailand published the results of Project Meridian FX APAC on 13 Nov. A prototype synchronisation operator built by Partior coordinated movements of central bank money so that both legs of an FX trade settle together (payment-versus-payment), and also ran multilateral net FX settlement, across test systems that included both real-time gross settlement (RTGS) and distributed-ledger platforms. The banks say it worked across different technologies and time zones, and that netting let banks use liquidity more efficiently. The BoE plans a live synchronisation interface in 2028.

So what: FX settlement risk (paying one currency and not receiving the other) is one of the oldest problems in cross-border banking. If synchronisation goes live, treasury and payments teams could settle Asian-currency trades in central bank money without a single shared ledger; watch for the BoE's 2028 interface specification.
stories.chip: Checked on the Bank of England's joint media release (opened); PYMNTS coverage matches
src: Bank of England, MAS and Bank of Thailand: joint release
stories.short: The Bank of England, Singapore's MAS and the Bank of Thailand tested a 'synchronisation' service that settles both legs of FX trades together in central bank money, across both traditional and ledger-based systems, and also netted trades between banks. The BoE plans a live synchronisation interface in 2028.

stories.title: Uber tells drivers that hackers stole personal and driver's licence data from a vendor, which TechCrunch identifies and Uber confirms as AI inference provider Fireworks AI; state notices list 7,870 people in Massachusetts, South Carolina and Rhode Island so far, with California and Illinois residents also notified, the same Fireworks breach that Cursor says led to its trojanised Claude Code extensions
stories.h: Fireworks AI hack spreads to Uber: drivers' licence data stolen
stories.ticker: Uber says driver licence data was stolen in the Fireworks AI breach
stories.body:
Uber is warning drivers that hackers stole their personal and driver's licence details from a vendor, which TechCrunch identified, and Uber confirmed, as AI inference provider Fireworks AI (via TNW). Uber says Fireworks told it on 9 Oct that internal credentials had been stolen. Notices to state attorneys general list 2,567 people in Massachusetts, 3,430 in South Carolina and 1,873 in Rhode Island, 7,870 so far; California and Illinois residents were notified without a count. Fireworks, valued at $17.5bn in July, has disclosed two October incidents and blames a group that sells stolen access to AI models ("LLMjacking"). It is the same breach Cursor says led to its tampered Claude Code extensions (Developing).

So what: a model-hosting vendor turned out to hold identity documents. Banks using third-party inference should ask what customer data their AI vendors keep, for how long, and whether it sits next to credentials attackers can resell.
stories.chip: Checked on TNW (TechCrunch's report, state counts, Fireworks' explanation); Uber's notices themselves not opened
src: The Hacker News: Cursor links its incident to Fireworks
stories.short: Uber says hackers stole drivers' personal and licence details from Fireworks AI, an AI inference vendor, after credentials were stolen in October. State filings so far list 7,870 affected people in three states, with more to come. It is the same Fireworks breach behind Cursor's tampered Claude Code extensions.

stat.label: Uber drivers notified so far, three states

stories.title: The top scorer in both rounds of South Korea's 2026 tax accountant exam, who got 397.5 of 400 with one wrong answer in 160, confesses through his lawyer that he photographed questions with a microcamera, sent them to a generative AI tool and read answers on a smartphone; Seoul police open an investigation days before Thursday's national college entrance exam (CSAT)
stories.h: South Korea's top tax-exam scorer admits he cheated with a hidden camera and AI
stories.ticker: Korea's top tax-exam scorer confesses to AI cheating; police investigate
stories.body:
The candidate who ranked first in both rounds of South Korea's tax accountant exam in April and July, scoring 397.5 of 400 with one wrong answer out of 160, confessed on 15 Nov that he cheated (The Guardian, Japan Times/AFP). He said he photographed questions with a microcamera, sent them to a generative AI tool and checked answers on a smartphone; he had earlier denied using smart glasses. Seoul police say they received a written confession and assigned investigators. The case lands days before Thursday's national college entrance exam, and education YouTubers are already urging tighter checks or a delay.

So what: professional certifications, including banking and accounting exams, rely on proctoring designed before cheap cameras and instant AI answers. Expect device detection, shorter windows and more oral or practical assessment.
stories.chip: Checked on The Guardian and The Japan Times (AFP): score, method, police statement
stories.short: The top scorer in South Korea's tax accountant exam, who got 397.5 of 400, confessed he photographed questions with a hidden camera, sent them to an AI tool and read the answers on a phone. Police are investigating, days before Thursday's national college entrance exam.

stat.label: score out of 400 in round one

stories.title: Estonia will close all border crossings with Russia from 1 December after eight people were detained over an attempted arson and explosion attack on drone maker Threod Systems, which Estonia's security service says Russia's GRU ordered; PM Kristen Michal links it to Estonia's support for Ukraine
stories.h: Estonia shuts every Russian border crossing after a GRU-ordered attack on a drone maker
stories.ticker: Estonia to close all Russia border crossings from 1 Dec after drone-maker attack
stories.body:
Estonia will close all its border crossings with Russia from 1 December, PM Kristen Michal said, after an attempted attack on Threod Systems, which makes long-range attack and reconnaissance drones (The Guardian). Eight people were detained on Saturday; no one was hurt and nothing was damaged. Estonia's internal security service, Kapo, says the attack aimed to cause an explosion and fire and was ordered by Russia's GRU military intelligence. Michal tied it to Estonia's support for Ukraine and said the closure sends "a clear message".

So what: sabotage against Europe's defence suppliers is moving from warnings to border closures. Firms with Baltic operations or Russian-border logistics should plan for the 1 Dec shutdown.
stories.chip: Checked on The Guardian (date, detentions, Kapo attribution, PM quote)
stories.short: Estonia will close every border crossing with Russia from 1 December after eight people were detained over an attempted arson and bomb attack on drone maker Threod Systems. Estonia's security service says Russia's GRU ordered it; the prime minister links it to support for Ukraine.

stories.title: Japan's economy contracts at an annualised 0.1% in July-September, government data show, against a median forecast of 0.3% growth, as consumption falters
stories.h: Japan's economy unexpectedly shrinks in the third quarter as shoppers pull back
stories.ticker: Japan Q3 GDP -0.1% annualised vs +0.3% expected
stories.body:
Japan's economy contracted an annualised 0.1% in July-September, government data showed on Monday, against a median forecast of 0.3% growth (Reuters via CNA); Reuters and Investing.com headline weaker consumption as the cause. Australian shares also slipped toward a one-week low on weaker copper and iron ore (Mint).

So what: a shrinking economy makes it harder for the Bank of Japan to keep raising rates while US yields sit near 5%; yen and Japanese bank stocks are the ones to watch this week.
stories.chip: Checked on CNA (Reuters copy: figure, forecast); the fuller Reuters story on Investing.com was blocked (403)
stories.short: Japan's economy shrank at an annualised 0.1% in July to September, government data showed on Monday, when economists expected 0.3% growth; weak consumer spending was the drag. It complicates the Bank of Japan's rate path as US yields stay high.

stories.title: OpenAI launches a science blog and details how GPT-6 Astra helped turn a candidate nonperturbative lattice definition of the Standard Model into a detailed proof; the underlying arXiv paper (2610.09093, Nathaniel Craig) constructs a gauge-invariant measure for overlap fermions in chiral gauge theories that include the Standard Model and ships a Lean formalisation
stories.h: OpenAI says GPT-6 Astra helped prove a step toward defining the Standard Model on a lattice
stories.ticker: OpenAI: GPT-6 Astra helped prove a lattice construction for the Standard Model
stories.body:
OpenAI opened a science blog on 15 Nov with a post on how GPT-6 Astra, its unreleased next model, "helped turn the idea into a detailed proof" of a candidate nonperturbative lattice definition of the Standard Model (OpenAI's feed summary; the page itself refused our request). The physics is in arXiv paper 2610.09093 by physicist Nathaniel Craig (6 Oct): it builds a gauge-invariant measure for overlap fermions on four-dimensional lattices for chiral gauge theories that include the Standard Model, a long-standing obstacle to simulating the theory from first principles. The paper (123 pages) comes with a Lean formalisation and calculation records.

So what: after maths results in August, this is the first time OpenAI has tied Astra to a frontier physics proof. The claim to check is how much the model contributed versus the author; the Lean files make parts of it checkable.
stories.chip: Checked on OpenAI's news feed (post title and summary) and the arXiv abstract and metadata; openai.com returned 403, so the post's description of Astra's role was not read in full
src: OpenAI: A step toward defining the Standard Model on a lattice
OpenAI: Our new blog for science
arXiv 2610.09093: A gauge-invariant measure for lattice chiral fermions
stories.short: OpenAI launched a science blog with a post on how its unreleased GPT-6 Astra helped prove a candidate lattice definition of the Standard Model of particle physics. The work, an arXiv paper by physicist Nathaniel Craig, ships with a Lean formalisation; how much Astra contributed is OpenAI's account.

stories.title: Attackers repurposed old, inactive Bitly short links in years-old posts by Burger King, McDonald's, Donald Trump and, per CNN, Bill Gates, Justin Trudeau, the FBI and the US Defense Department to redirect to unrelated content; Bitly confirms the issue, suspends the accounts and disables the links
stories.h: Old Bitly links in famous tweets were hijacked to send readers elsewhere
stories.ticker: Bitly confirms old short links were repurposed; accounts suspended
stories.body:
Old Bitly short links in years-old posts by Burger King, McDonald's and Donald Trump were found redirecting to unrelated pages (Ransomnews), and CNN reports the same for links from Bill Gates, Justin Trudeau, the FBI and the US Defense Department. Bitly said on X it had found an issue that "allowed bad actors to repurpose certain old, inactive links", suspended the accounts and is disabling the links. Ransomnews says 49 re-created links that mimic the originals still worked late on 15 Nov.

So what: banks and regulators have years of shortened links in statements, emails and posts. Each is a phishing path if a shortener lets it be re-pointed; audit old links and prefer your own domain.
stories.chip: Checked on Ransomnews' live-updated report (Bitly's statement quoted, CNN's additions); Bitly's post on X not opened
stories.short: Attackers re-pointed old, inactive Bitly links in years-old posts by Burger King, McDonald's, Donald Trump and, per CNN, the FBI and the Defense Department. Bitly confirmed the flaw, suspended the accounts and is disabling the links; some look-alike links still worked late Sunday.

stat.label: look-alike links still live late Sunday

stories.title: The FDA rejects Summit Therapeutics and Akeso's lung cancer drug ivonescimab, saying in its letter that the absence of an overall survival benefit does not support approval even though the drug slowed cancer progression; the decision was largely expected by analysts
stories.h: FDA rejects ivonescimab, the Chinese-born lung cancer drug that once beat Keytruda
stories.ticker: FDA rejects Summit/Akeso's ivonescimab: no survival benefit
stories.body:
The FDA rejected ivonescimab, a lung cancer drug from US biotech Summit Therapeutics and China's Akeso, Summit said on Sunday (STAT). The letter says the drug slowed cancer progression but did not help patients live longer, and that this "does not support the positive benefit-risk profile" needed for approval. Endpoints calls the rejection, in a narrow lung cancer setting, largely expected by analysts.

So what: the FDA is holding Chinese-originated drugs to overall-survival evidence, which matters for the many licensing deals Western pharma has struck with Chinese biotechs and for investors pricing them.
stories.chip: Checked on STAT (letter wording) and Endpoints (headline and opening; rest paywalled)
stories.short: The FDA rejected ivonescimab, a lung cancer drug from Summit Therapeutics and China's Akeso, because it slowed tumours but did not help patients live longer. Analysts largely expected it; the decision tests the value of Western licensing deals for Chinese-developed drugs.

stories.title: TSMC confirms in an SEC filing that current and former employees' data was posted online after a seller auctioned a claimed 6.9GB, 46,000-record dataset with national ID numbers and banking details; TSMC says the data matches records held by a cloud service provider and its own systems were not compromised
stories.h: TSMC confirms leaked employee data came from its cloud provider
stories.body:
TSMC told the SEC that some current and former employees' data was published without authorisation, and that it matches data stored with a cloud service provider; it has found no evidence its own systems were breached (BleepingComputer). A seller called "SmithBianl" had offered a claimed 6.9GB, 46,000-record set including national ID numbers, addresses and banking information, starting at 3 BTC, with a free-leak deadline of 15 Nov.

So what: staff bank details in a public dump mean targeted fraud; banks with TSMC payroll customers in Taiwan should expect impersonation attempts.
stories.chip: Checked on BleepingComputer (TSMC's SEC filing quote, seller's claims)

stories.title: IDBI Bank's officer and employee unions ask the RBI to withhold approval for the Rs 52,878 crore strategic sale of IDBI Bank to Fairfax Financial Holdings, seeking scrutiny of acquisition funding, beneficial ownership, Fairfax's control of CSB Bank and the valuation versus RBL Bank's sale to Emirates NBD
stories.h: IDBI Bank unions ask the RBI to hold up Fairfax's Rs 52,878 crore takeover
stories.ticker: IDBI unions urge RBI to withhold approval for Fairfax deal
stories.body:
Two IDBI Bank staff bodies, UFIOE and AIIBEA, asked the RBI on 15 Nov to withhold all approvals for the government's Rs 52,878 crore sale of control of IDBI Bank to Fairfax Financial Holdings (ETBFSI). They want independent checks on where the money comes from, ultimate ownership, whether IDBI's own deposits or assets could fund the deal, and Fairfax's existing control of CSB Bank. They compare the price with Emirates NBD's purchase of RBL Bank in June and cite IDBI's Rs 3.56 lakh crore of deposits.

So what: this is India's first big bank privatisation; how the RBI handles fit-and-proper and funding questions will set the template for future foreign-owned Indian banks.
stories.chip: Checked on ETBFSI (deal value, demands, deposits)

stories.title: Starling founder Anne Boden is building Lockwood, a UK bank for customers who use AI agents: users set spending limits per agent and out-of-limit payments are refused; it will offer a current account but no lending or savings, seek an e-money licence in 2027 and launch as a bank in 2028, self-funded for now, aiming for a million customers in its first year (Sunday Times interview via Sifted and Dealroom)
stories.h: Starling's founder is building Lockwood, a bank designed for AI agents
stories.ticker: Anne Boden's Lockwood: a current account with spending limits for AI agents
stories.body:
Anne Boden, who founded Starling, is building Lockwood, a bank she says will be "built by agents, to serve customers that want to use agents, and then be defended by agents" (Sunday Times interview, reported by Sifted and Dealroom). Customers would give each AI agent a spending limit, for example a £100 monthly grocery cap for a shopping assistant, and Lockwood would refuse anything outside it. It will offer a current account only, no loans or savings, start with an e-money licence in 2027 and become a bank in 2028. Boden is funding it herself for now and targets a million customers in year one.

So what: agent spending limits are becoming a product, not just a risk control (see ChatGPT Wallet and Wells Fargo's new terms). Incumbent banks will need per-agent mandates of their own.
stories.chip: Not opened: the Sunday Times and Sifted are paywalled or blocked; details from search snippets of Sifted, Dealroom and a fintech analyst's post

stories.title: Zelensky says Starshield, the military-grade Starlink service the US government provides Ukraine, is still running too slowly to intercept Russian missiles and drones, and urges the US and Elon Musk to lift the restrictions before winter attacks on the energy grid
stories.h: Zelensky urges the US and Musk to lift Starshield limits before winter
stories.ticker: Zelensky: Starshield slowdown hurts Ukraine's air defence
stories.body:
President Zelensky says Starshield, the military-grade Starlink service Ukraine uses to intercept missiles and drones, is still restricted and too slow, and that protecting the energy grid this winter "directly depends" on lifting the limits (BBC). He urged the US and Elon Musk to be "on the right side of history". The slowdown was first noticed in October; Musk has said the US government controls Starshield, while Trump said he told Musk to "put it back". It follows Zelensky's claim that the US floated Donbas-for-NATO (15 Nov).

So what: a private satellite network is now a lever in a war and in peace talks, ahead of the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting on 19 Nov.
stories.chip: Checked on BBC News (quotes, history of the dispute)

stories.title: The Pentagon renames its Chief Digital and AI Office (CDAO) the Super Intelligence Office, following Trump's executive order 14434 telling agencies to say 'Super Intelligence'; Cameron Stanley becomes Chief Super Intelligence Officer and the office's portfolio, including Maven Smart System, moves to SI.mil
stories.h: Pentagon renames its AI office the 'Super Intelligence Office'
stories.ticker: Pentagon's CDAO becomes the Super Intelligence Office
stories.body:
The Pentagon (now styled the Department of War) renamed its Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office the Super Intelligence Office on Friday (SecurityWeek). Cameron Stanley, a former Project Maven lead, is now Chief Super Intelligence Officer; programmes including the Maven Smart System targeting platform continue, and resources move to SI.mil. It follows Trump's September executive order 14434 telling agencies to use "Super Intelligence" instead of AI where the law allows.

So what: a rename, not new money, but contract language and vendor paperwork for US government AI work will start to change.
stories.chip: Checked on SecurityWeek (names, date, EO number)

stories.title: Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reports Apple plans to unveil Siri AI smart glasses at WWDC 2027 and ship them by the end of 2027; they rely on a nearby iPhone, lean on third-party app integration with Siri starting in iOS 27.3 beta, and prototypes are slightly thinner than Meta's second-generation Ray-Bans
stories.h: Apple plans to show Siri smart glasses at WWDC and ship them by end-2027, Bloomberg says
stories.ticker: Bloomberg: Apple smart glasses at WWDC 2027, shipping by year-end
stories.body:
Apple plans to unveil smart glasses at its next WWDC and ship them by the end of 2027, Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reports (via 9to5Mac). They will not run apps themselves but lean on a nearby iPhone, with Wi-Fi as a fallback, and Apple is laying groundwork for third-party apps in Siri from the iOS 27.3 beta. Test units are slightly thinner than Meta's second-generation Ray-Bans, with flush cameras and a use indicator light.

So what: Apple joins Meta and Google-Samsung (shipping 10 Dec) in AI glasses; a camera on every face raises the same bystander-privacy questions banks face for branch and trading-floor policies.
stories.chip: Checked on 9to5Mac's summary of Bloomberg's report; Bloomberg not opened

stories.title: Mirra Andreeva, 19, wins the WTA Finals on debut, beating Elina Svitolina 7-5, 6-3; at the ATP Finals in Turin, world No. 1 Alexander Zverev and Ben Shelton win their openers
stories.h: Mirra Andreeva, 19, wins the WTA Finals on her debut
stories.ticker: Andreeva beats Svitolina 7-5, 6-3 for the WTA Finals title
stories.body: Mirra Andreeva, 19, beat Elina Svitolina 7-5, 6-3 to win the WTA Finals at her first attempt, having also beaten her in the group stage (The Athletic). Svitolina had knocked out Aryna Sabalenka in the semi-finals. At the ATP Finals in Turin, world No. 1 Alexander Zverev beat Rafael Jodar and Ben Shelton beat Arthur Fils; Carlos Alcaraz plays Frances Tiafoe on Monday.
stories.chip: Checked on The Athletic live blog (scores, schedule)

stories.title: Olivia Cooke tells The Times that Slow Horses, Apple TV's spy drama, will end with its eighth season, which she is now filming
stories.h: 'Slow Horses' will end with season eight, Olivia Cooke says
stories.ticker: Apple TV's Slow Horses to end with season eight
stories.body: Olivia Cooke told The Times she is shooting the last season of Apple TV's spy drama Slow Horses, its eighth: "that's what we've been told and it definitely feels like we are ending" (Variety). Apple has not announced it. Also on Sunday: the Academy's Governors Awards gave honorary Oscars to Glenn Close and Ridley Scott, among others.
stories.chip: Checked on Variety (Cooke's quotes); Apple has not confirmed

stories.update: Bessent says Nvidia needs a 'dramatic shakeup' from outside and must explain whether it sold to China via shell companies; Huang agrees to testify to three House committees; Megaspeed says Alice Huang left in August 2025; earnings Tuesday.
stories.title: Treasury Secretary Bessent says Nvidia needs a 'dramatic shakeup' with outside leadership and must explain whether it knowingly let advanced chips reach China through shell companies linked to Megaspeed; Rep. Moolenaar says Jensen Huang has agreed to testify behind closed doors to the China select, foreign affairs and intelligence committees; Megaspeed says Alice Huang left in August 2025, denies wrongdoing and opens an internal probe; the FT reports Huang is discussing a comeback; bipartisan support grows for tighter chip-export rules; Nvidia reports earnings on Tuesday
stories.h: Bessent wants an outsider to run Nvidia as Huang agrees to testify
stories.ticker: Bessent calls for an outside Nvidia CEO; Huang to testify; earnings Tuesday
stories.body:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Fox News on Sunday that Nvidia needs a "dramatic shakeup" in leadership and suggested an outside CEO (Bloomberg via Japan Times). He wants answers on whether Nvidia used shell companies to sell chips above the H200 to China: "these shell companies were obvious" (CNA). Rep. John Moolenaar said Jensen Huang has agreed to testify, behind closed doors, to the China select committee and the foreign affairs and intelligence committees, so no subpoenas were issued (BBC). Megaspeed says Alice Huang left on 30 Aug 2025, denies wrongdoing and has hired outside counsel; Singapore says she was still in charge for most of 2025 (TNW). The FT reports Huang is discussing a return; his representative declined to comment. Speaker Mike Johnson sees "growing consensus" on limiting chip exports (The Verge), and The Hill reports scrutiny of Commerce Secretary Lutnick's role. Nvidia reports earnings on Tuesday.

So what: Tuesday's results now double as a governance test. Banks and funds with large Nvidia weightings face three risks at once: an outside CEO forced by Washington, tighter export rules, and a possible founder return.
stories.chip: Checked on BBC (testimony, Megaspeed), CNA (Bessent quotes), Japan Times/Bloomberg (shakeup, earnings Tuesday), TNW (Megaspeed dates) and The Verge (Congress); the FT comeback report was not opened (paywall)
src: The Verge: Congress and export rules
stories.short: Treasury Secretary Bessent says Nvidia needs a 'dramatic shakeup' with an outside CEO and must explain whether chips reached China via shell companies. Jensen Huang has agreed to testify privately to three House committees; Megaspeed says Alice Huang left in 2025. Nvidia reports earnings on Tuesday.

stories.update: Iran fires six drones at the US radar site at Riffa air base in Bahrain, its second attack in three days; Bahrain says all were intercepted, and Iran's speaker says a path to a deal remains open.
stories.title: Iran's Revolutionary Guards launch six drones at the US air-defence radar at al-Riffa air base in Bahrain on 15 Nov, the second attack on Bahrain in three days and the first on a Gulf state since September; Bahrain says it destroyed them, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Jordan and Egypt condemn the attack, the IRGC says the Strait of Hormuz is closed, and parliament speaker Ghalibaf says a path to ending the war is open on Iran's terms
stories.h: Iran fires drones at a US base in Bahrain for the second time in three days
stories.ticker: Iran drones target US radar in Bahrain; Bahrain says all intercepted
stories.body:
Iran's Revolutionary Guards say they launched six drones at the US air-defence radar at al-Riffa air base in Bahrain on Sunday, their second attack on Bahrain in three days (BBC). Bahrain says its air defences destroyed them "before they could achieve their objectives"; sirens sounded nationwide. The IRGC said "the Strait of Hormuz is closed". Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Jordan and Egypt condemned the attack (Guardian live). Parliament speaker Ghalibaf said a path to ending the nine-month war is open if the US accepts Iran's "logical conditions"; Trump said he may hold off on strikes absent new provocations (Bloomberg via Japan Times). An Iranian claim that a tanker with 2 million barrels sank in Hormuz (NDTV) is unconfirmed.

So what: attacks on Gulf hosts of US forces put a floor under oil prices even as the IEA sees a surplus; banks' Gulf exposures and trade-finance desks should watch shipping insurance rates this week.
